revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Field Day Ribbons
revealWordProblem.text: For Field Day, the PE teacher is ordering award ribbons and pin buttons. Ribbons come in packs of 7 and pin buttons come in packs of 10. She wants to buy the exact same number of ribbons as pin buttons, with none left over, and she wants to buy as few packs as possible. What is the fewest ribbons (and pin buttons) she can buy, and how many packs of each does that require? Explain how the LCM solves this.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The fewest number of ribbons and pin buttons she can buy is the LCM of 7 and 10. Since 7 and 10 share no common factors other than 1, the LCM is their product: LCM(7, 10) = 70. She needs 70 ÷ 7 = 10 packs of ribbons and 70 ÷ 10 = 7 packs of pin buttons, giving exactly 70 of each with none left over.

questions.stem: What is the LCM of 3 and 5?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, ... Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, ... The smallest common multiple is 15.
choiceFeedback: 3 is just one of the two numbers — it is not a multiple of 5. List the multiples of 3 and of 5 and find the first number that appears on both lists.
5 shows up when you count by 5s, but it does not show up when you count by 3s. Look for a number that is in both lists.
30 is in both lists, but it is not the smallest. Go back to the lists and stop at the first multiple they share.
hints: LCM is about MULTIPLES (counting UP by each number), not factors. You want the smallest number BOTH lists reach.
Skip count by 3s in one row and by 5s in another row, then scan for the first number that appears in both rows.
Write the 3s row: 3, 6, 9, 12, … Then start the 5s row: 5, 10, … Stop as soon as one number shows up in both rows.

hintsEs: El mcm se trata de MÚLTIPLOS (contar HACIA ARRIBA de cada número), no de factores. Buscas el menor número al que llegan AMBAS listas.
Cuenta de 3 en 3 en una fila y de 5 en 5 en otra, y luego busca el primer número que aparezca en las dos filas.
Escribe la fila del 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, … Luego empieza la del 5: 5, 10, … Detente en cuanto un número aparezca en ambas filas.

choiceFeedback: 48 = 6 × 8 is a common multiple, but not the least one — a smaller number is on both lists first. List multiples of 8 (8, 16, 24, ...) and stop at the first one 6 divides.
It looks like you added 6 + 8. The LCM does not come from adding: you need to find a number that appears in both lists of multiples.

hints: Careful: 6 + 8 is not a multiple of either number. You need a number that both 6 AND 8 divide into evenly.
List multiples of the LARGER number, 8, and check each one: is it also divisible by 6? Stop at the first hit.
Test 8: divisible by 6? No. Test 16: divisible by 6? No. Keep climbing the 8s list until a number divides evenly by 6.
questions.explanationEs: Múltiplos de 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, ... Múltiplos de 8: 8, 16, 24, ... El menor múltiplo común es 24.
hintsEs: Cuidado: 6 + 8 no es múltiplo de ninguno de los dos. Necesitas un número al que 6 Y 8 dividan exacto.
Escribe los múltiplos del número MAYOR, el 8, y revisa cada uno: ¿también es divisible entre 6? Detente en el primero que sí.

steps: 1. Skip count multiples of each number starting with the larger number
2. Identify the first non-zero multiple that appears in both lists
3. Prime factorization method: Product of highest powers of all prime factors
reviewHighlights.watchOut: A common mistake in Least Common Multiple is multiplying the two numbers together instead of listing multiples to find the smallest shared one. For example, for 4 and 6, a student calculates 4 × 6 = 24 and calls that the LCM, but the actual least common multiple is 12 (multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12; multiples of 6: 6, 12 — 12 is the first number that appears in both lists). This shortcut only works when the two numbers share no common factors (like 4 and 9, where the LCM really is 36 = 4 × 9); for numbers like 4 and 6 that share a factor of 2, multiplying overshoots the true LCM. Always list multiples of both numbers and pick the first one that appears in both lists.

level1.stem: What is the LCM of 2 and 7?
level1.explanation: Since 2 and 7 share no common factors (they are relatively prime), LCM = 2 × 7 = 14.
choiceFeedback: That is what you get if you halved the correct amount. Instead: Since 2 and 7 share no common factors (they are relatively prime), LCM = 2 × 7 = ___.
2 is a multiple of 2, but not of 7. The LCM can never be smaller than the larger of the two numbers.
It looks like you added 2 + 7. You find the LCM by counting multiples, not by adding the numbers.
hints: Notice that 2 and 7 are both prime — they share no common factor. That makes this a special, faster case.
List the multiples of 7 and find the first one that 2 also divides — in other words, the first EVEN multiple of 7.
Test 7: is it even? No. Move to the next multiple of 7 and check evenness again — stop at the first even one.
level1.explanationEs: Como 2 y 7 no comparten factores comunes (son primos entre sí), el MCM = 2 × 7 = 14.
hintsEs: Fíjate que 2 y 7 son ambos primos: no comparten ningún factor. Eso hace que este sea un caso especial y más rápido.
Escribe los múltiplos de 7 y busca el primero que 2 también divida, es decir, el primer múltiplo PAR de 7.
Prueba 7: ¿es par? No. Pasa al siguiente múltiplo de 7 y revisa si es par otra vez; detente en el primero que lo sea.

level1.stem: (Lesson 6.13) Which of the following is a prime number?
level1.explanation: 17 has exactly two factors: 1 and 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7, and 9 = 3 × 3, so they are all composite.
choiceFeedback: 15 = 3 × 5, so it has factors besides 1 and itself. A prime number has exactly two factors — test whether any smaller number divides your choice evenly.
21 breaks apart into 3 × 7, so it has more than two factors. Look for the number that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
9 splits into 3 × 3, which gives it a third factor besides 1 and 9. Keep checking each number for a hidden factor pair.
hints: Re-read what 'prime' means: exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Any extra factor makes a number composite.
Test each choice by dividing by small primes like 2, 3, 5, and 7. If anything divides in evenly, that number is composite.
Start with 9: since 3 × 3 = 9, it has a factor besides 1 and 9, so 9 is composite. Cross it off and test the next choice the same way.
level1.stemEs: ¿Cuál de los siguientes es un número primo?
level1.explanationEs: 17 tiene exactamente dos factores: 1 y 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7 y 9 = 3 × 3, así que todos son compuestos.
hintsEs: Relee qué significa 'primo': exactamente dos factores, el 1 y él mismo. Cualquier factor de más vuelve compuesto al número.
Prueba cada opción dividiendo entre primos pequeños como 2, 3, 5 y 7. Si alguno divide exacto, ese número es compuesto.
Empieza con el 9: como 3 × 3 = 9, tiene un factor además del 1 y el 9, así que el 9 es compuesto. Táchalo y prueba la siguiente opción igual.

level1.stem: (Lesson 6.13) What is the prime factorization of 30?
level1.explanation: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. All three factors (2, 3, 5) are prime, so 2 × 3 × 5 is the prime factorization.
choiceFeedback: That is what you get if you stopped too early — 6 is not prime, it still breaks down into 2 x 3 — re-read what the question is asking for.
You started the factor tree correctly, but 15 is not prime — it still splits into 3 × 5. Keep going until every branch ends in a prime.
This is a real factor pair of 30, but 10 is composite (10 = 2 × 5). A prime factorization can only contain prime factors.
hints: A prime factorization uses ONLY prime numbers. Look at each choice: are ALL of its factors prime?
Break 30 down step by step, and keep splitting any factor that is still composite until every factor is prime.
Start with 30 = 2 × 15. Is 15 prime? No — so split 15 into two primes and collect everything you found.
level1.explanationEs: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. Los tres factores (2, 3 y 5) son primos, por eso 2 × 3 × 5 es la factorización prima.
hintsEs: Una factorización prima usa SOLO números primos. Mira cada opción: ¿son primos TODOS sus factores?
Descompón el 30 paso a paso y sigue partiendo cualquier factor que todavía sea compuesto hasta que todos los factores sean primos.
Empieza con 30 = 2 × 15. ¿Es primo el 15? No — así que parte el 15 en dos primos y reúne todo lo que encontraste.

level2.explanation: LCM(15, 20) = 60 minutes. Both buses return together 60 minutes after 8:00 AM, at 9:00 AM.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. LCM(15, 20) = ___ minutes.
40 minutes works for Bus B (40 = 2 × 20), but 40 is not a multiple of 15, so Bus A has not returned yet. The moment has to work for both buses.

hints: Both buses start together at 8:00 — they meet again after a number of minutes that both 15 and 20 divide evenly.

hintsEs: Vuelven a coincidir en un momento que es múltiplo de 4 y también de 6: ese es el mínimo común múltiplo.
Escribe los múltiplos de cada número y busca el primer valor que aparezca en las dos listas.
Empieza las listas: 4, 8, ... para la primera máquina y 6, ... para la segunda. Sigue extendiendo las dos hasta que el mismo número aparezca en ambas.

level3.stem: One ship docks every 8 min, another every 12 min. They just docked together. In how many minutes do they dock together again?
level3.explanation: LCM(8, 12) = 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24; multiples of 12: 12, 24. The first shared multiple is 24 minutes.
choiceFeedback: Does both numbers divide into that evenly?
That's a common multiple, but is it the LEAST? Find the smallest one.
16 is a multiple of 8, but not of 12. Keep extending both lists until you find a number that is in both.
level3.stemEs: Un barco atraca cada 8 min y otro cada 12 min. Acaban de atracar juntos. ¿En cuántos minutos vuelven a atracar juntos?
level3.explanationEs: MCM(8, 12) = 24. Múltiplos de 8: 8, 16, 24; múltiplos de 12: 12, 24. El primer múltiplo compartido es 24 minutos.
hints: Both ships dock together at a time that is a multiple of 8 and also a multiple of 12.
Skip count by each number separately, then look for the first time the two counts land on the same value.
Multiples of 8 begin 8, 16, ... and multiples of 12 begin 12, ... Keep extending both lists until one number turns up in each.
hintsEs: Los dos barcos atracan juntos en un momento que es múltiplo de 8 y también de 12.
Cuenta salteado con cada número por separado y busca la primera vez que los dos conteos caen en el mismo valor.
Los múltiplos de 8 empiezan 8, 16, ... y los de 12 empiezan 12, ... Sigue extendiendo las dos listas hasta que un número aparezca en las dos.
